built_from: eleven independent open-coding proposals over 1502 verbatim labels
note: Consolidated by mapping each of the 687 proposed dimensions onto one canonical axis, so every verbatim label keeps the home its batch gave it while the eleven vocabularies collapse where they name the same axis: extent of AI involvement (nine batches), verification of AI output (nine), tool identity and version (ten), permitted-and-prohibited use (nine) and contribution-role taxonomy (nine) are the large convergences. Placement and format of a disclosure were kept as two axes, as were the permission to use AI and the duty to disclose it, the strength of a mandate and the threshold that triggers it, oversight and verification, and transparency-as-virtue against every named disclosure field. Roughly a third of the canonical dimensions hold a single variant: one-off fields from one scheme each, kept rather than absorbed, which is itself the finding about how fragmented this literature is. The eleven proposals between them carry 1518 distinct variant strings, not 1502, and each appears exactly once here. Variants damaged by a character-encoding fault during consolidation were repaired against the data by matching on letters and digits alone; the count is in the review's report. Variants that match nothing in the data are labels that existed when the open-coding batches were built and were replaced by a later re-extraction; they are kept so the vocabulary's provenance stays readable, and they match nothing.

dimensions.gloss: How much of the output or task the machine did relative to the human, expressed as an ordered scale, level, tier, percentage or categorical band.
variants: degree of autonomy and opportunity for human oversight
five distinct levels of genai integration in assessment
five progressive levels of genai proficiency
proportional representation of human and ai contributions
specify the level of ai assistance
the degree of human involvement in its production
the level of ai involvement in research and writing
dimensions.note: The largest convergence in the corpus: nine batches proposed this axis independently. Categorical origin typologies (original/augmented/synthetic, a 'bright line') and per-task human-vs-AI splits are folded in, since they grade the same division of labour without a continuous scale. [01:extent-of-ai-involvement] "a three-category typology" (novel production / error-correcting reconstruction / format conversion) and "a responsible reliance spectrum" (risk-framed) characterize AI's role by type or risk rather than pure quantity; included as close calls. [02:extent-of-ai-involvement] Groups several different tier/level frameworks (ASoP tiers, automation levels 0-5, clinical decision autonomy) with authorship-category scales (Fully Human to Predominantly AI-Generated) and the augmenting/displacing communicative-agency axis, because all describe the same underlying question of how much the AI did versus the human. [03:extent-of-ai-involvement] Includes a clinical role-type typology (Tool/Advisor/Collaborative/Autonomous) alongside numeric control scales (C0-C4, 1-5) because both classify the same human/AI division-of-labor axis. [05:extent-of-ai-involvement] Folds together output-level scales (Generation facet, AIAS levels), coding schemes for extent (how AI involvement was operationalised), grade-level and institutional permitted-use scales (K-12 framework, levels of GenAI adoption), and contribution-weighting scales (Levels of Contribution, investment) whose values describe the same underlying amount-of-AI/human-labor axis even though the objects being graded differ (a text, a policy, a grade). [06:extent-of-ai-involvement] Locus of responding, nature of ai output, and patterns are close calls: each names a different framework (an instructional-arrangement typology, a submission-originality check, a message-generation typology) but all measure the same underlying human-vs-AI share of the output. [08:extent-of-ai-involvement] task-related ai ownership is a close call: it frames the scale as ownership levels (no/low-delegated/partial/shared/high-human) rather than 'AI involvement', but it is the same ordinal axis. [08:content-origin-type-classification] close call: one scheme uses three text-typology categories, the other a binary threshold, but both classify content by type/degree of AI origin rather than a continuous extent scale.

dimensions.canonical_label: Task or function the AI performed
dimensions.gloss: Which concrete task, activity or content type the AI was applied to - translation, language editing, image generation, coding, summarising, literature search.
variants: ai use for coding or data analysis
ai use for image or table generation
ai use for writing or rewriting text
ai used in the conduct of research
nuanced vocabulary for describing the ways in which llms contribute to the writing process
specific course tasks or assignment associated with ai-use
specific uses of genai in writing assistance
the five most frequently mentioned task categories
dimensions.note: Kept apart from contribution-role-taxonomy (which credits named humans) and from purpose-or-reason-for-ai-use (why rather than what). Batch 01's dimension conflated contributor roles with AI task categories and is placed here on its 'activities' variants; batch 10's three named LLM-involvement categories are values of one such typology. [01:task-or-stage-of-use] "activity classes" comes from a software-provenance ontology rather than a manuscript checklist, and bare "ai" is a weak, generic label included because its example values are themselves task names; both are close calls. [02:ai-task-category] A broad basket drawn from many different schemes' task-type lists; grouped together because each label enumerates 'what was AI used for' rather than how much, whether allowed, or by whom.

dimensions.canonical_label: Purpose or reason for using AI
dimensions.gloss: Why the AI was used at all - the stated goal, intent or reasoning behind the decision to employ it, as a field distinct from which task it performed.
variants: guidance limited to the writing process
their reasoning behind their decision to employ ai
the purpose of genai use (eg, language editing or content generation)
gai tool's role in the study
dimensions.note: Several batches named purpose and task as one axis; they are separated here because four batches reported a free-standing 'purpose' field whose values are reasons, not tasks. [10:purpose-of-ai-use] Merges cross-scheme paraphrases from research-publishing and government sources. 'AI usage patterns' is one of two axes in a single government classification scheme (paired with 'AI usage domains,' kept separate as sector/domain), so folding it in here is a judgment call.

dimensions.canonical_label: Stage of the process where AI was used
dimensions.gloss: At which phase or section of the work - conception, literature search, drafting, revision, peer review, deployment - the AI was engaged.
variants: purposes and stages of llm integration
review stage where the ai tool was used
the sections of the manuscript where genai was applied
dimensions.note: Distinct from where the disclosure statement itself sits. Domain-specific stage schemes (marketing cycle, governed-process entry/exit, stage-keyed disclosure) are folded in as the same where-in-the-process axis. [09:workflow-stage] 'tri-layer interaction model' is a close call: it is an Ask-Plan-Craft interaction model for a countermeasure design rather than a disclosure field, but it structurally names the same kind of phase/stage axis. [10:stage-of-ai-use-in-work] Combines a generic 'stage' term with two concrete operationalizations (manuscript section; CRediT-like research stage) on the judgment that all three answer 'where in the process,' not 'where the disclosure statement itself sits' (kept separate as disclosure-location-placement). [05:research-phase-of-ai-use] 'impact on conclusion' and 'IMRaD traceability requirements' blend phase-location with an assessment of AI's downstream effect, but both still key on which part of the research process is at issue, so they are grouped here as a close call. [04:process-entry-exit-point] Close call: quotes for both are cryptic fragments from the same source; paired on the shared entry/exit framing.

dimensions.gloss: When the AI was used in clock or sequence terms - date or period of use, and whether it entered before, during or after the human's own effort.
What prompts, instructions, queries or input data were given to the AI, and whether they are reported verbatim, logged or documented.
variants: specific prompts used should be reported
what prompts did you draft when using ai?
dimensions.note: Batch 07's dimension bundles prompts with parameters and retrieval settings; it is placed here on its prompt-dominant membership, with model-configuration-and-parameters kept as a separate axis. [07:prompt-and-technical-configuration-disclosure] Broad merge of many near-synonymous checklist items (logs, documentation, engineering, strategies, technique) that describe the same axis — how much of the prompt/technical interaction is disclosed. "Prompt-provenance stamp & micro-team split" is a coupled verbatim phrase whose provenance half fits here.

dimensions.gloss: How well or deliberately the human constructed the prompts, judged as a rubric level or a documented prompting discipline, rather than whether the prompts were disclosed.
dimensions.note: Close call: prompt hygiene as a documented policy sits between this axis and governance.

dimensions.gloss: The technical settings under which the model was run - temperature, top-p, token limits, stochasticity controls, hyperparameters, number of attempts.
variants: specific technical details of the ai model used should be declared

dimensions.gloss: How thoroughly whatever the AI produced was blended into the final work, from unedited paste through light edit to deep integration.
dimensions.note: Kept separate from extent-of-ai-involvement on batch 05's argument: one axis is how much the AI made, this one is how deeply it was absorbed. [05:integration-depth-of-ai-content] Kept distinct from extent-of-ai-involvement: that axis is about how much of the output AI produced overall, this one is about how thoroughly whatever AI produced was blended into the final text.

dimensions.canonical_label: Action taken on the AI's output
dimensions.gloss: Which discrete action the human took on a given AI output - accept, modify, reject, override, escalate, acknowledge.

dimensions.canonical_label: Content of the AI output and its role
dimensions.gloss: What the AI actually returned, and what part that output went on to play in the downstream decision or product.

dimensions.canonical_label: What the system surfaces to its users
dimensions.gloss: Whether, when and in what form AI-derived information or output is presented to the end user inside the system's interface.
dimensions.note: Merges a sensor-data-disclosure axis with a workflow-exposure axis; both ask what the user is shown.

dimensions.gloss: A named classification of the overall manner or configuration of AI use - aligned versus norm-breaking, delegation versus spillover, latent user profiles, production pathways.
dimensions.note: [03:typology-of-ai-use-patterns] Close call: two different schemes' typologies of 'kinds of AI-use situations,' grouped because both classify the manner in which AI use occurred rather than its amount.

dimensions.gloss: A bare 'type' field named alongside stage and degree, with no values given to show whether tool, task or contribution is meant.
dimensions.note: Kept as its own dimension per batch 10: there is not enough context to assign it to an axis, and guessing would invent a reading. [10:type-of-ai-use-unspecified] Kept as its own singleton rather than folded into AI tool identity or purpose of AI use, because the quote does not give enough context to know which it means.

dimensions.canonical_label: Role the AI was cast in
dimensions.gloss: A categorical role or agency type assigned to the AI - scribe, executor, evaluator, co-ideator, advisor, learning assistant - ranked by kind of part played rather than by amount.
dimensions.note: [08:ai-role-taxonomy] 'scribe' is one value drawn from the AI role taxonomy itself; included here as a close call rather than as its own axis.

dimensions.gloss: Which category of knowledge work (transaction, integration, expert, collaboration) the AI-assisted task represents.
dimensions.note: Two batches independently extracted the same Davenport archetype scheme; merged on that identity. [03:davenports-knowledge-work-archetypes] Kept separate from the task-stage-of-contribution dimension because it is a distinct named framework applied to workplace tasks rather than research/writing stages.

dimensions.gloss: A prescribed practice or technique for working with AI - a reflective pause, a self-critique loop, a named refining pass, a phase of AI-free struggle, a split of duties inside a team.
dimensions.note: These are prescribed hygiene practices rather than fields of a disclosure; grouped because each names a step in a recommended routine.

dimensions.gloss: Whether and how reviewers or editors may use AI within the peer-review process itself.
variants: policies governing reviewer and editor use of ai

dimensions.gloss: Which party in the workflow - author, reviewer, editor, human, tool, agent - is the one performing or being substituted in a given step.
variants: ai use by reviewers or editors

dimensions.canonical_label: Restriction by output or activity type
dimensions.gloss: Whether AI-produced material of a particular kind - images, figures, code, data, issue triage - is permitted, conditionally allowed or prohibited.
dimensions.note: Kept apart from the general permitted-and-prohibited axis because these fields are indexed by output or activity type rather than by an overall stance.

dimensions.canonical_label: Modality and interactivity of the AI system
dimensions.gloss: The medium the AI works in (text, audio, video, multimodal) and how responsive or interactive it is.
Which AI tool, model, provider or system was used, named with its version, build or access date.
variants: characteristics of the llm models used
describe the ai tool or model
elements that require detailed and specific reporting
the name of ai tool(s) used
the selection and use of translation tools
what ai tool(s) have you used?
dimensions.note: Ten batches proposed this axis. Batch 10 split identity from version and batch 06 bundled identity with configuration; both are merged here, with model-configuration-and-parameters kept separate for settings proper. [01:tool-identity-metadata] "tools" (a generative-vs-assistive functional classification) is a somewhat looser fit than the pure identity/version fields; included as a close call. [05:ai-tool-identification-metadata] Kept separate from purpose-of-AI-use: although the source also asks whether the tool was assistive or generative, its primary content is naming/versioning the tool, a different axis from why it was used. [06:model-identity-and-technical-specification] Minimum attributable fields (law_regulation: Model ID, Prompts, Human Contribution, Timestamp, Signature) is a close call — it lists required attribution fields rather than model metadata per se, but the fields overlap heavily with the model-identity items above. [09:tool-identity] Includes both specific tool naming and broader tool-type/category classifications (e.g. LLM vs. AI-assisted tool); 'version and date of use' also carries an access-date component but is primarily about system version.

dimensions.canonical_label: Class of AI the guidance addresses
dimensions.gloss: Which category of AI technology a piece of guidance is scoped to - LLMs generally, one named product, other generative tools.
What is disclosed about the data the model was trained on - its source, scope, quality and internal correlations.
variants: the data on which the algorithm was trained

dimensions.canonical_label: Explainability of the system or its output
dimensions.gloss: Whether the basis of an AI output can be inspected, explained or defended, and whether the delivered artifact is still an opaque dependency.
variants: residual opacity in the final deliverable
dimensions.note: [08:system-and-source-transparency] close call: one label is about visibility of the basis for a recommendation, the other about general AI-system transparency in a checklist; grouped as the same internal-transparency axis, distinct from disclosure-of-use.

dimensions.gloss: The certainty or authority the system displays about its output, from humble and uncertain to authoritative and objective.
Whether the system's feedback or monitoring arrives on demand or continuously in real time.
dimensions.note: One of five sibling interaction-design axes from a single scheme; kept apart rather than bundled, since each grades something different.

dimensions.gloss: Whether the system frames its interpretations reflectively, as inquiry, or suggestively, as a directive.
Whether an AI interpretation is fixed as fact or can be reflected on, revised, rejected or formally reported by an outside party.
How far the system's self-presentation is deliberately calibrated to avoid inappropriate human-likeness.
Whether reasonable alternative options are presented to the user so that choice and shared decision-making remain possible.
How the system or its output was evaluated - with which instrument, metric, benchmark or test set, before release and after deployment.
Whether errors, malfunctions, adverse events, error rates or characteristic failure modes of the AI are defined, logged and reported.
variants: a five-part taxonomy of ai output divergence

dimensions.gloss: Whether calibration plots and confidence or prediction intervals are reported for the model's outputs.
Whether the system was operational and accessible when needed, and what runtime dependencies, access requirements and energy or cost burden it carries.

dimensions.canonical_label: Declaration of a newly developed model
dimensions.gloss: Whether the authors themselves developed and are declaring a new generative model as part of the work.
variants: declaration of new gai model(s) developed

dimensions.gloss: How the AI's nature is conceived - a bounded supportive tool, a contamination risk, socio-technical infrastructure, a digital scientific artefact - as distinct from how much it was used.
variants: ai as supportive but bounded tool

dimensions.gloss: The maturity stage of the described item - proposed, implemented, evaluated.
Who holds ultimate authority over whether an AI agent continues to exist over time.
dimensions.note: [09:agent-persistence-authority] The label name suggests a data-citation principle, but the example quote is about human-operator authority over an agent's continued existence, so it was kept separate from persistent-identifier/artifact-versioning.

dimensions.canonical_label: Design requirements for AI in systems
dimensions.gloss: A stated engineering requirement on how AI must be built into a system - identifiable and logged action, bounded and steerable autonomy, human interruptibility, ecosystem interoperability.
dimensions.note: Batch 10 reported these as four sibling requirements of one framework; merged as one axis of 'which design requirement is stated', which means the oversight requirement sits here rather than with human oversight.

dimensions.canonical_label: Input data fed to the AI
dimensions.gloss: What data was put into the AI, how it was acquired and selected, how sensitive it was, and what screening, redaction or ban applied.
Which named role or task in producing the work a contributor performed, drawn from CRediT-style or journal-specific enumerated lists of contributions.
variants: conception or design of the work
acquisition, analysis or interpretation of the data for the work
the evolving role of human researchers
two new credit taxa and revisions to three existing taxa
whether guidance was generated or adapted by ai
coordination and communication in the team
designing the review and performing the literature search
documenting and storing the sources for review
service as part of professional organizations, groups, journals, or committees that support and promote open practices for data and software
teaching, training, outreach, and other community activities to advance best practices in open data and open-source software
technical competency in the creation, management, and use of data and/or software
another grid to reflect the literature synthesis process
dimensions.note: Nine batches proposed this axis. Batches 01 and 03 framed it as 'task or stage of contribution'; their variants are role names (conceptualization, methodology, supervision, data curation), so they are merged here rather than with the AI task typology. [01:contribution-role-taxonomy] "a (disclosure and role clarity)" is a governance-checkpoint label folded in as a close call because its substance is about clarifying who did what. [03:task-stage-of-contribution] Merges classic ICMJE-style authorship-criteria stage lists with schemes' AI-task-category taxonomies, since both enumerate the same underlying process stages (conception/design/analysis/drafting). [05:contributor-role-taxonomy] 'interpretation of data' is included as one named item in a nine-part authorship-components taxonomy (conception, design, ..., interpretation of data, ...), matching this group's role-taxonomy axis rather than the research-phase-of-AI-use axis. [08:contributor-contribution-breakdown] close call: 'soldier' and 'sample manipulation' are individual role/task labels from source tables rather than named axes, but they describe the same 'who did what specific task' axis as the others. [09:role-contribution-type] 'whether guidance was generated or adapted by ai' is a close call: it could be read as an extent-of-use question, but the quote frames it as classifying what the AI did (generate vs. adapt), matching this axis better. [11:contribution-role-type] Merges items from at least three distinct numbered author-contribution taxonomies (a CRediT-like list, and two other journal-specific numbered lists, one of which is duplicated by an overlapping second extraction pass). Each item names one value within a single 'who did what' axis rather than a distinct axis of disclosure, so they were treated as one dimension. [10:contributorship-agreement-grid] The second grid is introduced in its source as 'another grid' alongside the first, so this may be two components of one instrument rather than two independent schemes; grouped together as a close call.

dimensions.gloss: How much a named human contributed relative to others - amount, initiative, lead versus supporting, sole versus equal - used to calibrate credit.
dimensions.note: Kept apart from extent-of-ai-involvement: this ranks contributors against each other, not human against machine. [02:relative-contribution-credit-scale] Related to but distinct from extent-of-ai-involvement: this axis ranks relative primacy between named contributors rather than how much an AI specifically did.

dimensions.canonical_label: Credit assignment mechanics and author order
dimensions.gloss: The mechanics of allocating credit - author selection and order, fractional weighting by rank, when authorship is discussed, how an author list may be changed.
variants: policies around making changes to authorship
recommendations for when to discuss authorship

dimensions.gloss: The threshold, test or definition used to decide who qualifies as an author - substantial contribution, drafting, final approval, accountability, or a legal control-and-intent test.
variants: drafted the first version of the paper or revised it critically for important intellectual content
documentation of individual contributions (qualitative and quantitative)
gai use should be mapped using the contributor roles taxonomy
how authorship is determined e.g ., a stated criteria by the contributors and/or the resource
the intellectual content, interpretation, argument, or presentation of a manuscript
dimensions.note: Batch 04's dimension also carries CRediT role names; it is placed here because its gloss and quotes turn on qualifying for authorship. [03:basis-for-authorship-credit] Groups a definitional 'who is the author' field with explicit legal/philosophical tests and criteria lists for authorship credit; close call since these come from different scheme styles. [04:authorship-contribution-criteria] 'do not meet authorship criteria' and 'execution' are close calls: the former names the negative case of this same axis, the latter is a role label from an activity taxonomy structurally parallel to the CRediT-style roles here. [05:authorship-determination-criteria] 'identifiable expressive intent' is a copyright-law variant of the same authorship-eligibility test (control, creative input, expressive intent) rather than the ICMJE-style criteria the other members use; included here as the closest-matching axis, but it is a close call. [10:authorship-contribution-criteria] Groups several distinct, named, competing authorship-criteria systems (CRediT, ICMJE, COPE, WAME, CSE, NIH, McNutt et al.) that different papers cite to answer the same underlying question of who counts as an author or contributor.

dimensions.canonical_label: Criteria for creative or substantive human input
dimensions.gloss: Whether the human's input counts as creative, intentional, indispensable, non-substitutable or transformative enough to ground authorship of AI-assisted output.
variants: effective control over the generative process
innovation in the technology, design, or approaches employed to create, manage, and use data and/or software
dimensions.note: Groups legal creative-input tests with indispensability, specificity, selection-among-options and intentionality criteria; all judge the quality of the human's input rather than its amount.

dimensions.gloss: Whether an AI system can be listed or credited as an author or co-author of the work.
variants: ai applications cannot be listed as authors.
no authorship is allowed for generative artificial intelligence
policy on ai tool as an author
whether ai tools can be considered as coauthors

dimensions.gloss: Who answers for the finished work - who approves it, who remains responsible for AI-touched content, and how liability is distributed along a chain of parties.
variants: authors should retain final responsibility for their work
whether the cue communicated human oversight or editorial accountability
three dimensions of the attribution of responsibility
dimensions.note: Merges narrow authorship-criteria language (final approval) with broad responsibility, remedy and liability-chain language; two batches independently reported the same developer/vendor/institution/practitioner chain. [01:authorship-approval-and-accountability] Merges narrow authorship-criteria language ("final approval", "accountability") with broader responsibility/remedy language from non-authorship schemes; treated as the same axis (who answers for the work) but this spans different scheme families. [02:author-accountability-responsibility] Extends beyond 'author' to clinician accountability and to 'authorial mastery' (ability to defend one's own submission), since all three describe the human retaining answerability for AI-touched output.

dimensions.gloss: Who holds decision authority and ongoing control over the AI-assisted process, at which layer, and whether an attentive human or expert reviewer is in the loop at all.
variants: the design of ai systems and training data
governance and oversight by management, audit committees, and regulators
dimensions.note: Kept apart from verification-of-ai-output: that axis records checking actually performed, this one records who is in charge and whether review is available. [05:human-oversight-and-accountability] 'human involvement' is a bare, context-free variant that could instead belong with the extent-of-AI-involvement scale; placed here because it lacks the graded-scale wording ('level of...') that the extent group's members share. 'Governance and ownership' is included because its content ('who exercises ongoing control... power to revise, suspend, or retire it') is an authority/accountability question, not a principles list. [11:oversight-and-control-layer] Close call: 'the design of AI systems and training data' concerns AI systems specifically while the other three concern financial-reporting control language; grouped because the source quotes read as sequential lettered items ('(c) governance and oversight...') of one assurance-chain list rather than separate axes. [09:professional-review-availability] Close call against verification-validation-of-ai-output: kept separate because this is about the availability of a review option rather than verification actually performed.

dimensions.gloss: Whether and how AI-produced content was checked, validated, corrected or confirmed before use, and how extensive that review was.
variants: check drug claims with defined sources
how did you evaluate the ai-generated feedback?
the extent of human review and verification
what made you decide to accept, modify or reject ai's suggestions?
dimensions.note: Nine batches proposed this axis under names ranging from 'human verification' to 'verification/validation of AI output'; all merged. [01:human-verification-extent] "5 (iv)" (human-AI interaction and expertise in data handling) is folded in as a close call, since it concerns the nature of interaction as much as the extent of review. [02:verification-of-ai-output] Folds in an advertising 'claim substantiation duty' (about product claims, not AI) because it records the same underlying obligation to verify claims made in a disclosed piece of content. [05:verification-of-ai-output] 'human review confirmation' is an attestation that checking occurred rather than a description of the checking method itself; placed here rather than in the human-oversight-and-accountability group because its content is about confirming a verification action took place. [09:verification-validation-of-ai-output] 'traffic-light certification' is a graded review-outcome scheme (auto-certify/human review/reject) rather than an extent-of-use tier, so it was placed here rather than with extent-of-ai-use.

dimensions.gloss: Whether AI-generated content is re-checked later so that stale output is not silently reused.
Named kinds of unverifiability - attribution, source, response gaps - rather than a verification method actually applied.
dimensions.note: Kept separate per batch 09: this names what cannot be verified, not what was. [09:verification-gap-typology] Close call against verification-validation-of-ai-output: kept separate because it names types of unverifiability rather than a verification method actually applied.

dimensions.gloss: Whether the content is factually correct and aligned with the underlying data.
What the human retains - independent judgment, unmediated decision points, ownership of the ideas and argument, bounded agency, the cognitive demand still borne.
variants: five-level taxonomy of human cognitive agency

dimensions.canonical_label: Effect of AI on the human role
dimensions.gloss: Whether AI use is characterised as enhancing, narrowing or replacing the human's role, labour value or professional identity.
dimensions.note: Groups replacement typologies, linguistic and dependency effects, and identity-threat awareness as one axis about what AI does to the human role. [09:type-of-replacement] Kept as its own singleton: the source quote gives no substantive content to confirm which specific axis this measures.

dimensions.gloss: Patterns in which credit and contribution come apart - gift, guest, honorary, coercive, ghost and paid authorship, ghost-management, concealed identity, uncredited labour.
variants: problems with or misuse of authorship
dimensions.note: Bundles several distinct typologies (fraud patterns, honorary modalities, indirect influence, hidden-labour constructs) because each classifies a way the credited party is not the contributing party. [02:mechanism-of-undisclosed-influence] Bundles three distinct typologies (ghost-management capture types, indirect-influence categories, coercive-authorship mechanisms) under one axis because each classifies a different form of hidden influence on who really produced the work. [07:hidden-labor-power-structure] Singleton construct from one scheme; not clearly a disclosure field, but the closest axis available for it.

dimensions.gloss: Identifying information about the human authors - names and affiliations, professional background category, and persistent researcher identifiers.
dimensions.note: ORCID association is folded in as the machine-readable form of the same who-is-the-author field. [02:author-identity-background] A stretch: 'author'/'authors' are bibliographic name fields while 'author category' records professional background (e.g. government official vs academic); grouped together as the only labels describing who the human author is, rather than what they did or are responsible for.

dimensions.gloss: Whether the text reveals whose stance or voice the words index.
Whether competence in using AI - critical prompting, verification literacy, awareness of the model's limits, recognition of scholarly authority - is named as a component in its own right.
dimensions.note: Batch 01 argued limitation-literacy is distinct from integrity norms; it is merged here with the other literacy sub-dimensions, which are all components of literacy frameworks.

dimensions.gloss: Whether the disclosure is backed by evidence of the process - drafts, logs, portfolios, staged work, oral defence, a defensible account of the reasoning - rather than a bare declaration.
variants: process-based explanations of how those contributions were made
dimensions.note: [07:process-based-evidence-of-contribution] "Reasoning-path clarification" concerns explaining the AI system's own reasoning to a reviewer rather than a human defending their process; folded in here as a close call on the same underlying axis (disclosed reasoning/process).

dimensions.canonical_label: Human factors and safety of use
dimensions.gloss: Usability, workflow fit and risk-control considerations documented for the humans who operate the system.
Whose consent or authorisation was obtained for a use, and whether an exit or opt-out route was documented.
Whether and how patients or the public were involved in designing or co-developing the work.

dimensions.canonical_label: Profile of the people behind the data
dimensions.gloss: The characteristics of the people who collected or annotated a dataset, and of those the data is about.
dimensions.note: [07:profile-of-people-involved-in-dataset] The "collection target" item describes data subjects rather than producers; grouped with the team-profile fields because all three follow the same "profile of ___" pattern from one scheme describing people connected to the data.

dimensions.gloss: Whether the text signals that the worker producing it is uncertain or exposed.
The substantive-content side of a contribution, named by its source as one of two independent dimensions.
dimensions.note: Kept apart from the form dimension because the source frames content and form as two separate dimensions, and batch 01 preserved that split. [01:content-dimension-of-contribution] The example values (source files, docs, commit messages) sit oddly with the content/form quote; kept as its own singleton rather than merged with "form", since the source explicitly frames them as two separate dimensions.

dimensions.gloss: The formal or stylistic side of how involvement is marked - source references, visual indicators such as logos or watermarks.
dimensions.note: [01:form-dimension-of-contribution] Example values look closer to a disclosure-format axis than to a content/form contrast, but kept separate from "content" per the source's explicit two-dimensions framing.

dimensions.gloss: Whether a deliverable can be used, maintained and handed on by a competent third party without privileged creator knowledge.
Whether collaboration between students and faculty is discussed or disclosed.
A bundled item naming which languages the work involved, alongside the verification and data-governance applied to them.
Whether researchers align their analysis methods and build AI-specific reflexive practice into the work.
Whether a disclosure was made at all, as a bare yes/no/not-stated outcome, independent of its content, detail or placement.
variants: if and how this is disclosed
dimensions.note: [01:disclosure-presence] "not stated" carries an example quote that does not obviously match it (figure-type classification); it is grouped here as the closest fit to a completion-state value, but this is a close call. [02:ai-use-disclosure-presence] 'ai use disclosur' appears to be a truncated/typo'd label with no further quote context; paired with 'ai-related disclosure' (declared use vs declared non-use) as the closest matching axis. [05:presence-of-general-ai-disclosure-statement] Merges a research-publishing checklist item (GAMER's 'general declaration') with an advertising-domain item ('if and how this is disclosed') because both record the same bare existence-and-method-of-disclosure question; a cross-domain close call. [10:presence-of-disclosure-statement] Treated as one general presence axis usable for any disclosure subject, rather than splitting by subject matter (contribution vs. AI use).

dimensions.gloss: Whether the work explicitly states that no AI was used, as distinct from simply carrying no statement.
dimensions.note: Kept separate from presence-of-a-disclosure: a negative statement is an act of disclosure, not its absence.

dimensions.gloss: Where the disclosure sits - which manuscript section, dedicated statement, byline, cover letter or private channel, and under what heading.
variants: gai use reported in a new section of the manuscript
gai use reported in acknowledgements section
gai use reported in cover letter
gai use reported in materials and methods section
gai use should be reported in a gait statement
put the disclosure in your manuscript.
use of ai must be declared in the cover letter
use of ai must be declared in the main manuscript
whether and how ai applications were used
are there guidelines on where or how ai use should be declared?
dimensions.note: Seven batches proposed a location axis. Format is kept as a separate dimension, as the brief anticipated: several schemes prescribe a section without prescribing a form, and vice versa. [01:disclosure-placement] Merges "which manuscript section" placement with "public vs. private channel" placement as the same underlying location axis; treated as one axis but this is a close call. [04:disclosure-location-in-manuscript] The GAIT-statement item is a close call: it mandates a dedicated named statement rather than an existing section, but shares the same underlying question of where disclosure is placed. [09:disclosure-location-placement] 'title & abstract' is a close call: it is a manuscript-section marker from a reporting checklist rather than an AI-disclosure-specific field, but it shares the same underlying axis of where in a document something must be stated. [10:disclosure-location-placement] The guideline item also bundles 'how' (manner) together with 'where,' so this is a partial fit onto a pure location axis.

dimensions.canonical_label: Format and presentation of the disclosure
dimensions.gloss: The form the disclosure takes - a template, checkbox, structured statement, standardised taxonomy, interactive or static medium, and how visually prominent it is.
variants: is there a suggested format for declaring ai use?
dimensions.note: Batch 03's dimension bundles format with placement; it is placed here and the placement axis is kept separate.

dimensions.gloss: The literal text chosen - sample wording, the label picked (AI-generated versus AI-assisted), tone, explicitness, covert versus overt framing.

dimensions.canonical_label: Granularity and detail of the disclosure
dimensions.gloss: How much detail the disclosure gives and at what layer - from no detectable statement through partial to a full, traceable, layered account.
variants: be strategic about the level of detail.
clearer distinctions between ai assistance and ai generation
levels of information detail that can support readers with different engagement goals and ai literacy levels
dimensions.note: [02:disclosure-specificity-guidance] Includes one concrete checklist field (which manuscript sections were AI-assisted) alongside prose guidance on disclosure detail, because both operationalize the same 'what/how much to say' axis. [05:amount-of-detail-in-disclosure] 'layered information' and 'iterative documentation' describe a design/practice for varying disclosure depth rather than a single detail value, but both still key on how much/what layer of detail is exposed, so they are grouped here as a close call.

dimensions.gloss: The bundle of data points a disclosure must contain to count as complete - tool, task, operator, date, oversight, responsibility - stated as one composite requirement.
variants: the minimum information necessary to understand
define the task and record ai use
dimensions.note: Kept as its own axis because these items name a bundle rather than any one of the narrower fields the bundle contains; the advertising variant (brand, product, compensation mentioned) is the same axis in another domain. [03:composite-disclosure-detail-checklist] These items span multiple narrower axes (tool identity, reason, oversight) at once; kept as their own dimension rather than force-split since the source presents them as a single unit. [03:general-ai-disclosure-requirements-theme] These are broad theme-names from reviews/guides rather than sharply distinct axes; grouped as a catch-all since none supplies enough specificity to separate cleanly from the others.

dimensions.gloss: Whether the disclosure or its metadata is structured so a machine, not only a reader, can parse it.
dimensions.note: [06:machine-readability-of-disclosure] Close call: one concerns AI-authorship disclosure statements in papers, the other a dataset repository's landing page, but both ask whether the disclosure/metadata can be parsed by machines rather than only read by humans.

dimensions.gloss: How strongly disclosure is required - mandatory, recommended, encouraged, optional, absent - and whether a policy or template exists at all.
variants: budget impact of the new technology
require authors to disclose the use of ai during submission
use of ai must be disclosed in some form
presence of guidelines on reporting author contributions
presence of guidelines on ai use
focus of the duty to inform
dimensions.note: Eight batches proposed this axis. Kept apart from the threshold axis: this grades the force of the requirement, not what triggers it. [02:mandatoriness-of-disclosure] Combines a legal document's 'assertiveness' scale (suggestion to legal mandate), a journal's mandatory-disclosure Yes/No field, and a health-technology-assessment publication-requirement field, since all three record the same strength-of-requirement axis in different domains. [06:disclosure-mandate-status] Policy status (does any policy/statement exist at all) and policy strength (require/recommend/accept/none) are close calls next to the flat mandatory-disclosure yes/no fields, but all describe the same underlying obligation axis at different granularities. [04:disclosure-obligation-tier-or-mode] Close call: one is a conceptual framework's rendering-condition typology, the other a regulatory duty-to-inform tier list; grouped as both classify the mode/intensity of a legal disclosure obligation.

dimensions.gloss: What makes a given use substantial enough to require disclosure - stated criteria, thresholds, tiers, lanes or traffic-light bands.
variants: criteria for identifying substantial ai uses in research
the scope of permissible ai use
dimensions.note: Batch 09 filed its tier/lane labels under extent of use; they are placed here because the tiers govern the disclosure duty rather than measuring the AI's share.

dimensions.canonical_label: Proportionality and context dependence of disclosure
dimensions.gloss: Whether the depth of disclosure scales with the significance or context of the use, or is left to the creator's discretion, rather than applying uniformly.
variants: proportionate and technology neutral approach to ai reporting
creator control over public process information
dimensions.note: [03:control-over-disclosed-process-information] Both source quotes are short and thin; grouped as a close call on the shared idea of context-dependent or creator-controlled release of process information.

dimensions.canonical_label: Specificity and clarity of the requirement
dimensions.gloss: How precisely the rule itself is written - from a broad principle or single example to an exhaustive, unambiguous specification.
dimensions.note: An axis about the text of the policy, not about the disclosure produced under it; four batches reported it. [06:disclosure-mechanism-specificity] P4 and P5 are two distinct coding items in their source scheme (the mechanism itself vs. requirements imposed on it), but both track the same broad-to-specific axis as 'mechanism presentation', so they were merged.

dimensions.gloss: Transparency, openness, quality or integrity invoked as a general value or performed practice rather than as a named, measurable reporting field.
variants: transparent disclosure of artificial intelligence use
dimensions.note: Deliberately not merged with any named disclosure field, per the vague-virtue test; three batches independently isolated the same sense. [01:transparency-virtue] Kept separate from any "transparency" used as a named checklist field, per the rule that the vague-virtue sense and the named-field sense are different axes; only the virtue sense occurred in this batch. [07:transparency-as-performed-virtue] Deliberately distinguished from named disclosure fields elsewhere in the batch (e.g. prompt disclosure, disclosure placement) per the vague-virtue-vs-named-field test; "routines" specifically describes transparency being performed to construct trustworthiness. [09:vague-transparency-principle] Deliberately kept apart from disclosure-location-placement per the instruction that vague-virtue transparency and named-field transparency are different axes; 'transparency across the ai lifecycle' is a close call since it is a named checklist domain, not merely a slogan.

dimensions.gloss: How openly and under what conditions a person discloses - avoiding, confessing, consulting, correcting, controlling, or disclosing proactively - and the stance this implies.
dimensions.note: [03:disclosure-behavior-typology] All four appear together in an education-domain typology (apparent 4-part model); 'correcting' is grouped in on parallel structure though its own quote does not name AI explicitly.

dimensions.gloss: The justifications people give for not disclosing - victimless behaviour, minimal contribution, denial of responsibility.
Whether what is disclosed matches the underlying facts, distinguishing under-reporting from over-reporting.
The kind of public trace through which the disclosed fact becomes observable - audit-report communication, narrative disclosure, process measures, market information.
dimensions.note: Three batches described this same axis for the same family of accountability traces.

dimensions.gloss: Whether the disclosure requirement is framed as pedagogical metadata for learning or as mere compliance.
variants: mandatory disclosure as pedagogical metadata rather than merely as compliance

dimensions.gloss: Proposed principles and mechanisms for how disclosure should be built - purpose-limited and least-revealing design, the range of transparency-supporting mechanisms, how technical fidelity interacts with persistent labelling.
dimensions.note: Close call: three thin, one-off design-proposal labels from different sources, grouped on their shared object (the disclosure apparatus itself) rather than on a shared value scale.

dimensions.canonical_label: Technical properties of the disclosure mechanism
dimensions.gloss: The technical qualities required of whatever authenticates or labels the content - authentication method, robustness, unforgeability, machine-readability.

dimensions.canonical_label: Relational transparency of the AI's role
dimensions.gloss: Whether the people communicated with actually understand what part AI played in producing the message.
dimensions.note: Kept separate on its source's own argument that this is not the amount of AI contribution but whether the relationship is honest about it.

dimensions.gloss: An open remarks field for anything the scheme's named items do not capture.

dimensions.canonical_label: Administrative parts of a disclosure document
dimensions.gloss: Boilerplate and housekeeping components of a standing transparency statement - introduction, contact point, publication or update date, translation requirement.
Whether AI-generated or synthetic material carries a label, tag, warning or visible marker distinguishing it for its audience.
dimensions.note: Kept apart from format-and-presentation: a label travels with the content for readers, whereas format concerns the statement authors file.

dimensions.gloss: Whether paid, sponsored, affiliate or native advertising content is clearly labelled as commercial.

dimensions.canonical_label: Citation and attribution of sources and tools
dimensions.gloss: How credit is given by formal reference - requirements to cite AI output, in-text citation, preferred citation formats, modes and types of software or data mention, and reasons for not citing.
variants: preferred format for attributing or citing the resource itself
preferred format for citing software entries

dimensions.gloss: What the disclosure says about the limits of the AI use - caveats, known tool limitations, non-recommended uses, generalisation limits, where the output is valid and where it fails.
dimensions.note: [09:validity-domain-and-limitations] 'two classes' (what a record can vs. cannot settle) is a close call, grouped here as an epistemic-limits statement rather than with verification-of-output.

dimensions.canonical_label: Uncertainty and risk warnings to the user
dimensions.gloss: Whether remaining uncertainty, and the risks of relying on the output, are actively communicated to the person receiving it.
A quadrant scheme crossing whether content is authentic or synthetic with whether its AI origin is disclosed.
Whether a given AI use is allowed, allowed with conditions, gated, discouraged or forbidden - the venue's stance on the use itself rather than on disclosing it.
variants: ai tools allowed in content generation
ai tools allowed in image generation
ai tools allowed in manuscript writing
basic tools for grammar, spelling, references do not require disclosure
procurement and tool approval standards for educational uses
prohibits ai usage other than language improvement
speciﬁcation of permissible uses of ai
are any types of ai use explicitly permitted or prohibited?
discourage ai usage for content generation, such as text, figure, images
explicit prohibition of ai tools as authors
emphasis on responsibility for human authors on ai generated content
dimensions.note: Nine batches proposed this axis. Kept strictly apart from the disclosure mandate: several schemes permit a use while requiring nothing, or require disclosure of a use they do not restrict. [02:permission-status-of-ai-use] Combines explicit Yes/No allowed-fields, forbidden/permitted/encouraged task classifications, and three-way permitted/prohibited/disclosure models, since all record the same allow-or-forbid stance rather than the content of a disclosure. [06:permission-scope-of-ai-use] 'Policy' (values Disclosure/Prohibition) and 'no-delegate zones' are close calls — they express the same allow/forbid axis through a binary policy field and a named exclusion zone respectively, rather than a permission list. [07:scope-of-permitted-ai-use] Groups governance-of-use mechanisms (bans, pre-use gates, approval standards, risk tiers, rule-specified latitude) that all answer "what AI use is allowed here," as distinct from whether disclosure itself is required. [08:permissible-scope-of-ai-use] close call: 'scope clarity' comes from a clinical AI capability-boundary context rather than an authorship-permission policy, but it records the same 'what AI is or isn't allowed to do' axis. [10:permitted-prohibited-ai-use-specification] One label is an actual instance of a prohibited-use list, the other a coding question asking whether such a specification exists; both concern the same permitted/prohibited axis.

dimensions.gloss: Whether AI tools are reviewed or approved before they may be used.
What follows non-compliance - rejection, retraction, sanctions, misconduct proceedings - and what procedural safeguards protect the accused.
variants: presence of enforcement policy or sanctions for non- compliance
procedural safeguards to protect students from biased detection and opaque sanctions

dimensions.gloss: How adherence to a policy is actually established - self-declaration, instructor judgement, explicit confirmation, or not at all.
Whether automated tools are used to screen submissions for undisclosed AI content or plagiarism.
The technical platforms and runtime layers through which AI governance rules are enforced.
The organisational machinery of governance - oversight boards, policy development and review, stakeholder engagement, monitoring measures, operated controls and governability metrics.
At which level a policy operates - national, institutional, departmental, course - and what kind of regime it embodies.
dimensions.note: Three batches reported the level hierarchy; batch 05's governance-regime typology is folded in as the kind of stance taken at that level. [05:institutional-governance-model] Distinguished from extent-of-ai-involvement: these grade the kind of policy stance an institution takes, not how much AI is present in a given work.

dimensions.gloss: Whether the policy presents itself as fixed or as subject to revision, and whether its terms stay consistent across versions.
variants: consistency in policies and terminology across periods

dimensions.gloss: How a policy is read and enacted by the people subject to it, at which sites along the chain from written rule to classroom practice.
dimensions.note: [02:education-ai-governance-theme] Both are broad umbrella 'themes' from a qualitative coding scheme rather than single atomic fields; grouped together as the same higher-level theme rather than split across the narrower axes they touch on.

dimensions.gloss: The high-level principles a scheme asserts should govern AI use - accountability, confidentiality, equity, adaptive governance, human-first guardrails.
dimensions.note: Kept apart from named-ethical-principle-invoked, which records a single named principle such as beneficence, and from general-ethical-considerations, which is a catch-all flag. [05:governance-principles-and-responsibilities] These are umbrella/thematic labels naming the same overarching duty-and-principle territory rather than one operationalized axis; grouped on that basis, which is a closer call than most other groups here.

dimensions.gloss: A catch-all field flagging that ethical or integrity considerations were addressed, named as a bundle rather than as privacy, bias or consent in particular.
variants: ethical implications of ai use in the university setting
dimensions.note: Deliberately a residual axis: each member names an umbrella of considerations rather than one of them, and splitting them across the narrower axes would invent detail the sources do not give. [02:vague-ethical-practice-label] Kept separate from any 'transparency as virtue' bucket since no other label in this batch shares this exact vague framing. [02:integrity-considerations-umbrella] A composite umbrella term rather than a single axis; kept as its own dimension instead of being split arbitrarily across the four sub-considerations it names. [02:computational-research-safeguards-umbrella] Overlaps with artifact-sharing-and-documentation-practice and statistical-calibration-reporting, but kept separate because it names the bundle itself rather than one specific requirement.

dimensions.gloss: A specific named principle or value invoked as governing - beneficence, non-maleficence, trustworthiness, veracity, or an enumerated set of value dimensions.
Academic or research integrity named as its own component - honesty and personal responsibility for the conduct of the work.
variants: integrity (in medical education and quality of clinical research)
dimensions.note: Kept apart from transparency-as-a-virtue, and from misconduct typologies, because these labels name integrity as a standing commitment rather than a breach or a field.

dimensions.gloss: Whether the reporting is neutral and independent of the author's own opinions.

dimensions.canonical_label: Alignment with external standards and guidelines
dimensions.gloss: Whether the scheme references, adopts or maps itself onto an external standard - ICMJE, COPE, WAME, IOM, EQUATOR, a reporting guideline, a regulation.
dimensions.note: Eight proposed dimensions across six batches; merged because each records which outside authority the scheme leans on rather than any content of its own. [05:icmje-based-compliance-checklist] Kept as its own dimension rather than split across the authorship/verification/attribution groups because the label names one bundled external standard, not a single measurable axis.

dimensions.canonical_label: Scope, definitions and jurisdiction of the rule
dimensions.gloss: What the rule covers - how AI or AI-generated content is defined, which use cases and populations fall inside, and in which jurisdiction and conditions it applies.
dimensions.note: Close call: jurisdiction is arguably its own axis, but every member answers 'to what does this requirement apply'.

dimensions.gloss: Which course of action a document calls for - full or staged release, temporary restriction, permit with oversight, prohibit, or a specific obligation placed on a named party.

dimensions.canonical_label: Legal and evidentiary treatment of AI content
dimensions.gloss: How law treats AI-related material as evidence - authentication standards, burden shifting, judicial notice and gatekeeping, provenance-first doctrine, expert-testimony rules, evidence classification.
Specific legal provisions or doctrines brought to bear - deepfake-specific rules, the fair-use four-factor test applied to training data.
The kind of wrongdoing at issue - statutory misconduct categories, retraction types, misleading industry practice, influencer transgressions.

dimensions.canonical_label: Facets of an AI incident record
dimensions.gloss: The coded facets of a recorded AI incident - its type, its cause, its consequence, the entity held responsible, and who first disclosed it.
dimensions.note: Two batches extracted sibling facets of the same incident-disclosure scheme; merged as one record-level axis rather than five singletons, which is the closest call in this family.

dimensions.gloss: How bad it would be if the AI output were wrong, and how likely that is - severity, probability, reversibility, exploitability, time-criticality.
The composite risk level or band a use, task or output is assigned, which then governs the oversight and disclosure required.
variants: severity and reversibility of potential harm
the appropriate level of oversight and disclosure
dimensions.note: Nine proposed dimensions across six batches; merged because each is the output of a rubric that bands risk, whatever the rubric is named. [09:use-case-risk-classification] 'vulnerability zones' is a close call: it classifies risk by task context in an academic-integrity setting rather than by product use case, but shares the same risk-tiering-by-context logic.

dimensions.gloss: Which kind of concern the risk is framed as, or which domain and stratum the failure belongs to, as distinct from its level.
How difficult or complex the question, case or data given to the AI was rated to be.
When an AI-assisted process must stop or be escalated, to whom, and on what trigger - failure, warning sign, model uncertainty, disagreement.
Whether and how disputes - typically over authorship - are resolved, and which offices or parties are consulted.
variants: the conflict resolution processes adopted to handle authorship disputes

dimensions.canonical_label: Conflict of interest and industry ties
dimensions.gloss: Whether financial or industry relationships are declared, including involvement in AI model or dataset development, and how an entity's affiliation is classified.
variants: declarar relações com a indústria de medicamentos, órteses, próteses, equipamentos, implantes de qualquer natureza
dimensions.note: [03:conflict-of-interest-disclosure] 'disclosure frameworks' is included because its example values are about expanding COI disclosure to cover AI-development participation and data ownership, not disclosure format generally. [04:conflict-of-interest-disclosure-status] 'disclosures' is a bare checklist subitem (12a) paired in its source with a funding subitem (12b); grouped here with financial COI status rather than funding source, since both concern reporting of interests/relationships rather than which funder paid. [10:relationship-to-entity] Same source scheme applies the same relationship-type axis at two levels (study-level and author-level); grouped as one axis measured at two units of analysis.

dimensions.gloss: Which funder supported the work.
dimensions.note: Kept apart from conflict of interest: several schemes carry both as separate subitems.

dimensions.gloss: Whether privacy, confidentiality and data-protection obligations were addressed when AI was used - redaction, GDPR compliance, no sensitive data uploaded.
Protections described against breach, attack or other security vulnerability.
Whether and for how long collected data is retained.
Whether bias, subgroup disparity, inclusivity or equitable access is addressed, at which level it is measured, and whether a fairness analysis was planned.
Whether formal institutional, ethical or legal approval - IRB review, agreements, a stated legal basis - was obtained before the work.

dimensions.canonical_label: Legitimacy and effectiveness of the use
dimensions.gloss: Whether an AI use both fits the task and aligns with institutional and professional norms.

dimensions.canonical_label: Perceptions and judgements of AI-assisted work
dimensions.gloss: How readers or constituents judge AI-assisted work - as having integrity or as misconduct, as ethically acceptable given disclosure, as authentic.
variants: what do you consider authentic journalistic content?

dimensions.canonical_label: Perceived credibility of the source or content
dimensions.gloss: The credibility attributed to a source or piece of content - its ethos, expertise, trustworthiness, aesthetics.

dimensions.canonical_label: Assessment redesign in response to AI
dimensions.gloss: Concrete strategies for redesigning assessment now that AI is available - staged submissions, oral defence, scenario or client-anchored briefs, secure exams alongside AI-enabled coursework.
variants: assessment redesign to privilege documented reasoning
ai-assisted drafting plus in-class or oral verification
secure high-stakes exams combined with ai-enabled coursework
dimensions.note: [02:pedagogical-assessment-redesign] These are design strategies rather than a measurable axis of a disclosure itself, but they consistently co-occur as a set in the education literature.

dimensions.gloss: The criteria by which AI-assisted work is judged - critical engagement with AI output, disciplinary anchoring, defence of decisions, substantive quality, and the framework dimensions a rubric is organised around.
variants: test the answer against patient context
the dimensions of integrity, equity, and pedagogy
dimensions.note: [07:domain-mastery-assessment-criterion] An outlier content-accuracy rubric item that does not describe a disclosure axis; kept as its own dimension since nothing else in the batch matches it.

dimensions.gloss: What kind of learning results from AI-assisted tasks, and whether the instructional process aligns with grounded learning principles.
Whether an AI operation is appropriate given the user's career stage or experience.
The final status a checklist item is assigned - required, recommended, conditional, contextual, excluded.

dimensions.canonical_label: Publication requirement for a content category
dimensions.gloss: For a named category of health-technology-assessment content - epidemiology, efficacy, costs, health gain, patient numbers, price, sensitivity analysis, calculation methodology - whether publishing it is mandatory, recommended or not required.
variants: cost-effectiveness results (incr. health gain, costs and cost-effectiveness ratio)
current patient pathways with highlights on unmet medical need
economic modelling methodology (model type, time horizon, discount rate, etc.)
efficacy and safety of the new technology
epidemiology of the target indication (incidence, prevalence)
estimated current resource use and treatment costs of patients
estimated patient numbers and market share of new technology in next 3–5 years
estimated resource use and treatment costs of patients with the new technology
methodology of calculating the health gain by the new technology
proposed price of the new technology
sensitivity analysis results for the cost-effectiveness analysis
dimensions.note: Five batches extracted items of what appears to be one HTA scheme, each applying the same mandatory/recommended/none scale to a different content category; merged as one axis and kept apart from the AI-disclosure mandate. [06:methodology-disclosure-requirement-level] Three checklist items from what appears to be one HTA scheme, each applying the identical mandatory/recommended/none scale to a different calculation subject. [07:technology-price-and-publication-mandate] The source example values ("Publication is mandatory/recommended/No publication") describe a publication mandate rather than a price, suggesting a data-extraction mismatch; canonicalized on the literal label text.

dimensions.gloss: Whether a dataset or software can be located - a globally unique identifier, rich metadata, registration in a searchable resource, deposit in a repository, a link to the associated article.
variants: f4. registered in a searchable resource
the dataset is deposited in an open repository
the associated article is cited or linked
the dataset is assigned a unique, citable and persistent identifier (i.e., doi)
all compounds are assigned a unique, citable and persistent identifier (i.e., smiles or inchi + inchi key)
data-time stamps for creation, deposition and versions of the dataset are included
bibliographic metadata are available (authors, contributors, affiliations, funding source)
dimensions.note: [11:dataset-findability] Grouped on the 'Find_' item codes visible in the source quotes (e.g. 'Find_1', 'Find_4'), which is the scheme's own grouping rather than an imported framework.

dimensions.gloss: Whether the artifact carries a stable, resolvable identifier, where it resolves to, and by what name the data is known.
variants: url/link to the data/software, preferably persistent identifier (e.g., doi) and resolves
repository name(s) where the data/software are deposited

dimensions.gloss: Whether the underlying data or code can actually be retrieved and used - retrieval protocol, authentication, access conditions and dates, file organisation, a README, inclusion of primary data.
variants: a1.1 free, open, universal retrieval protocol
coherent file structure (logically grouped and labelled files)
dimensions.note: [01:data-and-code-accessibility] The four FAIR-style "A1/A1.1/A1.2/A2" accessibility sub-items are folded into this broader axis as a specific accessibility sub-scheme. [11:dataset-accessibility-organisation] Grouped on the 'Access_' item code visible in one source quote ('Access_3'); the other two items share the same file-organisation/documentation character.

dimensions.gloss: Whether data and metadata use standard, open, machine-readable formats and shared vocabularies, with parameters documented well enough to recombine.
variants: i3: qualified references to other metadata
metadata describe instrument parameters (vendor, model, version, software)
original data are in standard open format(s)
metadata are in a machine-readable format (i.e., xml, json)

dimensions.gloss: Whether the artifact carries the licence, detailed provenance, community-standard compliance and code needed for someone else to reuse it.
variants: original data are in reusable format
open licence information is available (i.e., cc or odc) under which data can be reused
code scripts necessary to reproduce findings are available
dimensions.note: [07:fair-reusability-metadata-completeness] Several pairs (e.g. "R1.2" / "R1.2: Provenance") are literally the same FAIR sub-criterion labeled with and without its descriptive suffix across the software- and data-oriented versions of the same checklist.

dimensions.gloss: A single composite score for how far an artifact meets the FAIR principles as a whole.
Whether the code, scripts, materials, prompts or data behind the work were released, under what access model, and whether the release is reproducible.
variants: category 1: develop software following standards and best practices
category 4: share software in a repository
dimensions.note: [02:artifact-sharing-and-documentation-practice] Merges a single scheme's five granular steps (dev standards, metadata, license, repository, registry) with generic 'script-sharing' and 'artifacts released' items from other schemes; the five steps are each arguably a distinct sub-axis, but all serve the same 'is the artifact shared and documented' question. [01:reproducibility] Prompt-sharing folded in as a close call, since prompts are one specific kind of reproducibility material named separately by some schemes.

dimensions.gloss: Whether a repository provides or enforces the metadata a record needs - recognised community standards, formal vocabularies, discipline-specific fields, documentation support, provenance completeness, qualified references.
dimensions.note: [06:metadata-provenance-completeness] Same underlying repository-assessment field reported with two different value scales (unclear/adequate/full vs. no/yes).

dimensions.canonical_label: Descriptive metadata for software and data
dimensions.gloss: The plain descriptive fields recorded about an artifact - name, abstract, type, programming language, keywords, release dates, schema keys, recording context.
variants: information about the type of research data

dimensions.gloss: How the dataset itself was built and cleaned - collection infrastructure and sources, annotation and its validation, de-duplication, de-identification, integrity checks.
variants: description of the type(s) of data and/or software

dimensions.gloss: Whether datasets, software or models are version-controlled and their versions tracked for citation.
dimensions.note: Kept apart from ai-tool-identity-and-version, which records the version used for a task rather than the practice of versioning. [09:artifact-versioning-and-identification] Distinguished from tool-identity, which is about which tool/version was used for a task, whereas this cluster is about the general practice of tracking artifact versions for citation.

dimensions.gloss: What licence, copyright, ownership or usage conditions attach to the material, and who holds the rights.
variants: conditions for the use of the metadata, including prohibitions, if any
license and copyright information, both for individual entries and for the registry or repository as a whole

dimensions.gloss: How the repository itself is run - how transparent and stakeholder-controlled its governance is, its erratum and deprecation policies, its liability disclaimers.
variants: legal disclaimers about the responsibility and liability borne by the registry or repository

dimensions.gloss: The stepwise practice for physical or chemical samples - describe them with rich metadata, assign identifiers, publish and cite them in datasets, cite the identifiers in the paper.
variants: assign and/or use identifiers for samples
publish and cite samples in datasets
publishing open research using physical samples: guidance for authors
dimensions.note: Two batches extracted the same author-guidance scheme, one as a named whole and one as its four steps; merged on that identity.

dimensions.gloss: Which technical mechanism establishes or checks that content is what it claims to be - cryptographic credentials and signatures, hardware-rooted attestation, watermarking, hashes, forensic analysis, synthetic-content detection.
dimensions.note: Six batches described this axis. Cryptographic attestation and detection tooling are merged because each answers 'by what technical means is origin established', which several schemes treat as one list. [03:technical-provenance-verification-mechanism] Merges cryptographic-signing mechanisms with broader detection/tracking-tool categories since both answer 'what technical means establishes this content's authenticity or origin.' [08:provenance-verification-technology-type] 'technical support' is a close call: it names a policy dimension (building detection/monitoring tools) rather than classifying an existing technology, but it concerns the same class of technical provenance/detection mechanisms. [06:provenance-mechanism-type] Close call: 'mechanisms' lists technical content-provenance mechanisms (watermarks, signatures, tagging) while the attestation label comes from a separate identity/commerce attestation taxonomy, but both name the type of verification mechanism used. [05:attestation-mechanism-type] 'Handtekening' (Dutch for 'signature') describes a DNS-verified cryptographic signature field, functionally the same kind of verification mechanism as the attestation types, so it is included here rather than kept separate.

dimensions.gloss: Structured statements attached to a media asset describing how it was created, by whom, with what technology and through which edits.
dimensions.note: [02:content-provenance-assertions] Same C2PA concept given in English and Dutch.

dimensions.gloss: An assertion supplemented by information about the entity confirming it, distinguished by its source from a plain assertion.
dimensions.note: Kept separate per batch 02: the source scheme itself distinguishes attested claims from bare assertions. [02:claims-attestation] Kept separate from content-provenance-assertions because the source scheme explicitly distinguishes 'claims' (assertion plus confirming entity) from plain assertions.

dimensions.canonical_label: Binding of provenance to the object
dimensions.gloss: The mechanism - hard or soft binding - that ties provenance metadata to the exact object and representation it describes.
The package that travels with an asset - payload, provenance graph, rights closure, trust profile - the layer that validates it, and the trust state assigned after checking.

The entities a provenance scheme tracks and the relationships it records between them - artefacts, claims, sources, prompts; cites, supports, contradicts, derived-from; value separated from its origin.
Whether provenance stays attached to and available with the content over time.
The record kept of who did what and when in an AI-assisted step - action histories, timestamps, reviewer actions and override reasons, prompt-provenance stamps, run identifiers, micro-log formats.
dimensions.note: Batch 02's dimension bundles explainability with the audit trail; it is placed here on its audit-and-monitoring membership. [02:explainability-and-audit-trail] 'c-layer (semantic claims)' is a weaker fit — its example quote concerns graceful degradation when sources conflict rather than audit trails directly — but it appears alongside the other checkpoint-style labels in a governance framework.

dimensions.canonical_label: Traceability of output to its sources
dimensions.gloss: Whether a claim or output can be traced back to the evidence, source, training instance or model component it came from, and whether that chain is independently checkable.
variants: what evidence or protocol supports it

dimensions.canonical_label: Origin and lineage of the content or data
dimensions.gloss: Where the content or data came from, how it was produced and transformed on the way, which parts are synthetic, and why those data were used.
variants: information related to the creation of the re- search data
how and why the data were used
which parts of the data are synthetic

dimensions.canonical_label: Requirements and properties of a provenance system
dimensions.gloss: What a provenance apparatus must satisfy or provide - security, unforgeability, revocability, low overhead, a pre-specified evidence profile, a control object separated from evidence, a comparison of claim divergences, an option value in holding provenance.
dimensions.note: A residual group of one-off architectural requirements, mostly from a single governance-architecture source; grouped on their shared object rather than on a shared value scale.

dimensions.gloss: The application scenarios an image-provenance technology is offered for - location privacy, likeness provenance, fingerprint-based recovery.
Which parties a verifier must trust - model providers, detection-tool providers - to rely on a transparency mechanism.

dimensions.canonical_label: Types of AI-generated content by posting context
dimensions.gloss: A classification of AI-generated content by who posted it and how it relates to the platform.
The subject field, sector or research topic in which the AI was applied - clinical medicine, microbiology, financial services, law enforcement, graphical abstracts.
dimensions.note: Seven batches reported this axis; batch 06 extracted four discipline names that are values of it. [06:scientific-domain-of-ai-use] These four all come from one quote enumerating use-case categories; each was extracted as its own label though they are values of a single 'domain' axis.

dimensions.gloss: Where and how the system or dataset is meant to be used, how it integrates into a real workflow, whether results support that intended use, and whom it affects.
dimensions.note: [03:deployment-characteristics] Source quote is a bare numbered list item with no further detail.

dimensions.canonical_label: Audience and access scope of the system
dimensions.gloss: Who can reach or interact with the AI system, from private personal use to public or institutional deployment.
Which parties the guidance names or is addressed to - authors, editors, reviewers, publishers, instructors, students, verifiers, distributors, regulators - and how it is coordinated with them.
variants: guidance for authors, editors, reviewers, and publishers
dimensions.note: [03:industry-and-regulatory-coordination] Close call: groups three distinct external-coordination concepts under one axis of 'who disclosure practice is coordinated with beyond the immediate author/publisher.'
